idiom_name: class implements Target, holds private final Adaptee
implementation_notes: Java cannot inherit two classes, so the object adapter is the idiom: implement the target interface and hold the adaptee in a private final field (constructor injection, Objects.requireNonNull), translating each member and mapping exceptions into the target's vocabulary. A class adapter is possible only when the target is an interface and the adaptee a class (extends Adaptee implements Target), which welds the adapter to that concrete adaptee. For single-operation targets the adapter collapses into an anonymous class or, since Java 8, a lambda or method reference; Java 9 added in-place adaptation as a default method (Enumeration.asIterator()). The JDK ships finished adapters too: InputStreamReader and OutputStreamWriter bridge bytes to characters, Arrays.asList presents an array as a List, and Collections.enumeration presents a Collection as an Enumeration.
pitfalls: Checked exceptions are part of the adaptee's contract but not of the target's: wrap or map them deliberately instead of rethrowing vendor exceptions the target does not declare.
Returning adaptee types (the vendor's response object) re-couples callers to the vendor; map into target-owned types.
A class adapter extends the adaptee, so its public and protected members leak through the adapter; prefer composition when exposing those members is not part of Target.

Closing the adapter closes the wrapped stream (InputStreamReader.close() closes the underlying InputStream): decide at the boundary whether that is intended, or you will close something another component owns.

variants.name: Functional-interface adapter (lambda / method reference)
variants.implementation_notes: When the target interface is a functional interface (a single abstract method), the adapter collapses into a lambda, a method reference or an anonymous class: the JDK adapts any method to Runnable, Callable, Comparator, Executor or Supplier without a named wrapper, and Java 9+ adds in-place adapters as default methods inside the interface itself (Enumeration.asIterator()). Use it for single-operation targets and for short-lived wiring; write the explicit class when the target has several operations, needs its own state, or the translation must be documented and tested as a unit.
variants.idiom_name: Runnable r = this::run; Supplier<String> s = adaptee::getName;
variants.code_sketch:
Executor executor = this::handleTask;        // method -> Executor
Supplier<String> name = adaptee::getName;    // adaptee method -> Supplier

interface PaymentGateway { Receipt charge(long cents); }   // target
PaymentGateway gateway = cents -> adaptee.charge(cents, "USD"); // lambda adapter
pitfalls: `this::run` captures the enclosing instance, so a lambda stored in a long-lived adapter can leak it (and an Activity on Android).
A lambda cannot throw checked exceptions the functional interface does not declare; wrap in an unchecked exception or declare a dedicated interface.
Lambdas are anonymous in stack traces and carry no state; if the adapter needs a name, logging or several operations, write the class.
